s: The crucible nobody can replace
w: Silicon is pulled from a melt held in a fused-quartz crucible, and that crucible must be purer than the silicon itself or it poisons the crystal. Only a handful of deposits on Earth yield quartz clean enough, and the best of them is a small district around Spruce Pine, North Carolina.
h: Pegmatite ore is crushed, floated, acid-leached and chlorinated to strip alkali metals down to single-digit parts per million.
Grades are sold by impurity budget — IOTA-class material runs around 99.998% SiO₂ with aluminium under 8 ppm.
Crucibles are consumables: each Czochralski pull degrades one, so demand scales directly with wafer output.
Synthetic quartz from silicon tetrachloride exists but costs several times more and has not displaced natural HPQ for crucibles.

s: Copper, tin, tungsten, tantalum, cobalt, gold
w: A data centre is mostly metal. Copper carries current in the chip's back end, in the busbars, in the cables and in the transformers; tin solders everything; tungsten plugs vias; tantalum makes the barrier that stops copper from diffusing into silicon.
h: Copper demand from AI infrastructure is additive to electrification — a single high-density rack can contain 100 kg of copper before you count the cabling.
Tungsten and tantalum are conflict-mineral regulated, so provenance auditing is part of the supply chain.
Ruthenium is entering the interconnect stack as copper resistivity worsens at tiny dimensions; annual global supply is measured in tens of tonnes.
Gold is used in bonding wires, connector plating and package leads — small mass, high criticality.
k: copper in one high-density AI rack
share of cobalt refining that runs through China
x: Not scarce in the ground, but refining is concentrated and lead times for copper-intensive electrical gear now run past two years.

s: Rare earths, gallium, germanium, graphite
w: A short list of elements with no easy substitutes and one dominant refiner. Neodymium and dysprosium make the magnets in fans, drives and actuators; cerium polishes wafers; gallium and germanium make the compound semiconductors inside every optical transceiver.
h: China refines the overwhelming majority of rare earths and roughly 98% of primary gallium, and has run export licensing on gallium and germanium since 2023.
Cerium oxide is the abrasive in chemical-mechanical planarisation, the polishing step repeated hundreds of times per wafer.
Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride handle the frequencies and voltages silicon cannot — RF front ends, laser diodes, power stages.
Germanium goes into silicon-germanium transistors, fibre preforms and infrared optics.
Western capacity is being rebuilt from recycling and mothballed mines, but qualification runs years behind announcements.
k: China's share of primary gallium refining
expiry of the suspended US-specific ban
x: The clearest deliberate chokepoint in the chain. Controls are used as leverage and reversed as leverage; supply is available but permit risk is permanent.

s: Nitrogen, argon, helium, neon, hydrogen
w: Fabs are enormous consumers of gas. Bulk nitrogen purges and blankets everything; argon is the plasma workhorse; helium cools and leak-tests; neon is the lasing medium in deep-ultraviolet lithography and briefly became a war story in 2022.
h: A large fab consumes bulk gases on a scale that justifies an on-site air separation unit owned by the gas supplier.
Neon is a by-product of steel-industry air separation — Ukraine supplied a large share before 2022, and prices moved by an order of magnitude.
Helium has no synthetic route; supply tracks a handful of natural gas fields with helium-rich reservoirs.
Ultra-high-purity delivery is its own engineering discipline: electropolished stainless, point-of-use filtration, continuous particle monitoring.

s: Ultra-pure in the fab, evaporative at the data centre
w: Two very different water problems sit at opposite ends of this chain. A fab needs ultra-pure water — deionised past the point where it becomes chemically aggressive — for rinsing wafers. A data centre needs bulk water to reject heat.
h: A leading-edge fab can draw tens of millions of litres a day, with most sites now recycling well over half of it.
Ultra-pure water is produced through reverse osmosis, ion exchange, UV oxidation and degassing, then polished at point of use.
Data centre water use is measured as WUE, litres per kWh of IT load; evaporative cooling trades water for electricity and closed-loop designs do the reverse.
Siting decisions increasingly hinge on water rights and community consent as much as on power.
k: water draw of a large leading-edge fab
x: Not a technical constraint so much as a political one. Water is the most common trigger for local opposition to both fabs and data centres.

s: Gas, uranium, sun, wind, coal
w: Everything above this line is a way of turning primary energy into ordered information. Smelting silicon, running a fab, and training a model are all electricity-intensive to a degree that shows up in national statistics.
h: Metallurgical silicon smelting is one of the most energy-intensive steps in the entire chain, at roughly 12–14 MWh per tonne.
Fabs run continuously and cannot tolerate voltage sags; a momentary dip can scrap weeks of work in progress.
Data centre load is flat and around the clock, which suits nuclear and gas and stresses systems built for variable renewables.
Fuel choice increasingly determines where compute can physically be built, not just what it costs.
k: projected global data centre demand by 2030
load shape of an AI training cluster
x: Abundant globally, scarce locally and on schedule. The constraint is deliverability to a specific substation by a specific date.

s: Eleven nines of nothing else
w: Quartz is carbothermically reduced to metallurgical silicon at around 98% purity, then converted to a gas, distilled, and re-deposited as polysilicon pure to eleven decimal places. Electronic-grade material is a different product entirely from the solar-grade polysilicon that dominates by tonnage.
h: The Siemens process converts silicon to trichlorosilane, fractionally distils it, then decomposes it onto heated seed rods over days.
Electronic grade targets 11N purity — roughly one unwanted atom per hundred billion.
Fluidised-bed reactor granular polysilicon is cheaper and less energy-hungry but has struggled to hit electronic-grade specs.
Solar demand sets the price of the shared upstream; electronics buys a small, jealously guarded slice at a large premium.
k: duration of a single Siemens deposition run
x: A handful of Western and Japanese plants make electronic grade. Chinese capacity dominates solar grade but has limited qualified electronic-grade share.

s: Acids, solvents, and polishing compounds
w: Hundreds of litres of hyper-pure acids, bases and solvents pass over each wafer lot. Contamination budgets are counted in parts per trillion, so the bottle, the tubing and the filter are as engineered as the chemical inside.
h: Sulphuric, hydrofluoric, phosphoric and nitric acids do cleaning, oxide strip and selective etch; each has its own purity grade ladder.
CMP slurries are engineered colloids — ceria or silica abrasives plus oxidisers and inhibitors tuned per material layer.
Post-CMP cleans and photoresist strippers are separate specialty chemistries with narrow supplier lists.
Point-of-use filtration to sub-10 nm and continuous metrology are part of the delivered product.
x: Japanese and Korean specialty chemical firms hold decisive share in several categories — the 2019 Japan–Korea trade dispute made that dependency very visible.
co: Filtration, materials handling, advanced deposition materials

s: The molecules that become the chip
w: Every deposited film starts as a designer molecule. Tungsten hexafluoride becomes tungsten plugs; trimethylaluminium becomes alumina one atomic layer at a time; a growing family of metal-organic precursors enables materials that ordinary chemistry cannot deposit conformally.
h: Atomic layer deposition alternates two self-limiting precursor pulses, so film thickness is set by cycle count rather than by time.
Etch gases — fluorocarbons, chlorine, bromine chemistries — are tuned per material for selectivity and profile control.
Many precursors are pyrophoric, corrosive or both, so delivery hardware and abatement are part of the sale.
Precursor design is now co-developed with equipment makers and foundries years ahead of a node.
k: per ALD cycle, self-limiting by design
x: Narrow supplier lists per molecule, and switching requires full requalification of the process — so incumbency is extremely sticky.

s: The quiet recurring revenue of a fab
w: Sputtering targets, electrostatic chucks, showerheads, edge rings, quartzware, filters and pumps wear out on schedule. Consumables and spares are a large, unglamorous and highly qualified market that determines fab uptime.
h: PVD targets are high-purity metal discs — copper, titanium, tantalum, cobalt, ruthenium — consumed as film is sputtered off them.
Chamber components must survive plasma without shedding particles, which drives exotic coatings and ceramics.
Quartz and silicon carbide parts are refurbished and recertified in a specialised aftermarket.
Vacuum pumps and abatement systems handle gases that would be lethal or corrosive if released.
k: share of tool cost recovered in consumables over life
x: Diffuse and competitive, but individual part qualifications are single-source in practice.

s: One crystal, 200 kilograms, no grain boundaries
w: A seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon and withdrawn while rotating, pulling out a single cylindrical crystal in which every atom sits on the same lattice. Modern 300 mm ingots weigh a couple of hundred kilograms and take days to grow.
h: The Czochralski method controls diameter by pull rate and temperature, with magnetic fields used to damp convection in the melt.
Dopants are added to the melt to set base resistivity; oxygen and carbon levels are tightly specified.
Float-zone growth makes even purer crystal for power devices but cannot reach 300 mm economically.
Ingots are ground to diameter, notched for orientation, and characterised before slicing.
k: standard wafer diameter for logic and DRAM
mass of a modern 300 mm ingot
time to pull a single crystal
x: 450 mm was abandoned as uneconomic, so wafer area per pull is effectively frozen — one reason capacity expansion means more tools, not bigger wafers.

s: The flattest thing you can buy by the box
w: Ingots are sliced by diamond wire, then lapped, etched, and polished until surface variation is measured in nanometres across 300 millimetres. Flatness matters because lithography focuses to within tens of nanometres.
h: Wire sawing loses a significant fraction of the crystal as kerf; slurry and wire chemistry are optimised to reduce it.
Double-side polishing and final chemical-mechanical polish set the nanotopography the scanner will see.
Epitaxial wafers add a defect-free crystalline layer on top, needed for many logic and image sensor processes.
Every wafer is inspected for particles, crystal-originated pits and edge defects before it ships.
k: typical surface roughness after final polish
wafers in a standard FOUP carrier
x: Four suppliers cover most of the world's 300 mm demand. Qualification at a leading-edge fab takes years, so share moves slowly.

s: Where silicon cannot go
w: Silicon cannot emit light efficiently or switch at the voltages a data centre power stage needs. Indium phosphide makes the lasers in optical transceivers; gallium nitride and silicon carbide make the power electronics; sapphire and others serve niches.
h: InP is the substrate for the electro-absorption modulated lasers and DFB lasers in high-speed optics.
GaN-on-Si is displacing silicon in high-frequency power conversion, improving efficiency in server power supplies.
SiC dominates high-voltage traction and grid applications and is spilling into data centre power.
Substrate diameters lag silicon badly — InP is still largely 3–4 inch, which caps optics output.
k: efficiency targets driving GaN adoption in PSUs
x: InP substrate and laser capacity is the real ceiling on optical transceiver output — and transceivers are the ceiling on cluster scale-out.

s: Licensed instruction sets and cores
w: Almost nobody designs a CPU from a blank sheet. Arm licenses cores and the instruction set that runs most of the world's compute; RISC-V offers a royalty-free alternative that has become strategically important in China and in accelerators.
h: Arm licenses at two levels: ready-made cores, and architecture licences that let a customer build their own compliant design.
Every hyperscaler's data centre CPU — Graviton, Axion, Cobalt, Grace and Vera — is an Arm design.
RISC-V is modular and extensible, which suits domain accelerators where the control processor is a small part of the die.
GPU IP for mobile and embedded is a separate licensing market from data centre GPUs.
k: share of smartphones using Arm-based application processors
in NVIDIA's Vera CPU, an Arm v9.2 design
the RISC-V ISA itself is free to implement
x: Arm sits under nearly every mobile and an increasing share of server designs. RISC-V exists partly because that dependency makes governments nervous.

s: Compiling intent into geometry
w: Electronic design automation turns a hardware description into a manufacturable layout: synthesis maps logic onto standard cells, place-and-route arranges billions of them and wires them up, and sign-off tools prove the result meets timing, power and manufacturability rules.
h: Static timing analysis must prove every one of billions of paths meets setup and hold across process, voltage and temperature corners.
Place-and-route at advanced nodes is now heavily machine-learning assisted, exploring floorplans no human would try.
Sign-off includes design rule checking, layout-versus-schematic, electromigration, IR drop and thermal analysis.
A leading-edge tape-out consumes enormous compute — EDA is itself one of the larger HPC workloads on Earth.
k: vendors cover essentially the whole leading-edge flow
of timing paths checked per sign-off
of cluster time for a full physical implementation run
x: Three American and European vendors are a hard prerequisite for any advanced chip. Adding EDA to export-control lists is the single most effective lever available.

s: Proving it works before it exists
w: Silicon respins cost tens of millions of dollars and months of schedule, so most of a chip project's effort goes into proving correctness. Formal methods, constrained-random simulation, hardware emulators and FPGA prototypes all attack the same problem.
h: Emulators are purpose-built machines that map a full chip design onto reconfigurable hardware, running orders of magnitude faster than simulation.
Firmware, drivers and even operating systems are brought up on emulation months before first silicon.
Formal verification proves properties exhaustively rather than sampling with tests, and is standard for cache coherence and security blocks.
Post-silicon validation and debug close the loop with on-die instrumentation.
k: cost of a leading-edge mask respin

share of chip project effort spent on verification
x: Emulation hardware is expensive, capacity-constrained and export-controlled — a quiet bottleneck for anyone building large accelerators.

s: The contract between designer and fab
w: A process design kit is the fab's process expressed as models, rules and standard cells. Design-technology co-optimisation is the practice of changing the process and the design together — cell architecture, fin or sheet counts, track heights — because neither alone gets the win any more.
h: Compact device models capture measured transistor behaviour across corners and feed every simulation.
Standard cell libraries are the vocabulary of digital design; track height and pin access dominate density at advanced nodes.
Design rules encode what lithography and etch can actually resolve, including complex multi-patterning colouring constraints.
New nodes ship early PDK versions years before production so that lead customers can start designing.

s: When one die is not enough
w: Reticle limits and yield economics make giant monolithic dies impossible, so designs are split into chiplets connected by very wide, very short links. UCIe standardises the interface so that dies from different sources can be composed.
h: Die-to-die links trade distance for width: thousands of wires at low swing, delivering terabytes per second at a fraction of the energy per bit of a package-level link.
Splitting a design lets each function use the node that suits it — logic on the newest, I/O and analog on a mature, cheaper process.
Yield improves because smaller dies have fewer killer defects, and known-good-die testing becomes essential.
SerDes and HBM PHY IP are among the most valuable blocks in the industry.

s: Turning a layout into something light can print
w: The shapes a designer draws are not the shapes written onto a mask. Optical proximity correction, sub-resolution assist features and inverse lithography solve an inverse physics problem: what mask pattern, through this optical system, produces the intended silicon?
h: OPC distorts every edge to compensate for diffraction, etch bias and resist behaviour.
Inverse lithography technology solves for the ideal mask directly and produces curvilinear shapes that only multi-beam writers can make.
A single advanced layer's mask data can run to hundreds of gigabytes and take a large cluster days to compute.
Computational lithography is one of the largest private GPU workloads outside AI itself.
k: mask data volume for one advanced layer
cost of a single advanced EUV mask
x: Computational lithography is dominated by the same three EDA vendors plus ASML's own software — and it is compute-hungry enough to be capacity-limited.

s: The negative, written by electrons
w: A mask is a quartz plate with an absorber pattern that the scanner projects onto the wafer. EUV masks are different animals: reflective multilayer stacks rather than transmissive plates, protected by a pellicle membrane thin enough to pass extreme ultraviolet light.
h: Mask blanks are deposited with 40-plus alternating molybdenum/silicon layers to reflect 13.5 nm light, then patterned with a tantalum-based absorber.
Multi-beam electron writers expose the pattern, taking many hours per mask and enabling curvilinear shapes.
A single particle on a mask replicates onto every die of every wafer, so pellicles and handling are existential.
EUV pellicles must transmit around 90% of the light while surviving hundreds of watts of source power.
k: Mo/Si bilayers in an EUV mask blank
cost of one advanced EUV mask
x: Blank supply is dominated by two Japanese firms. There is no second source for EUV-grade blanks at volume.

s: A tin droplet, shot twice, 50,000 times a second
w: There is no lamp that emits 13.5 nm light, so one is manufactured. Molten tin droplets fall through a vacuum chamber; a CO₂ laser hits each one with a pre-pulse to flatten it, then a main pulse vaporises it into a plasma hot enough to radiate extreme ultraviolet.
h: Droplets are generated at roughly 50 kHz and must be hit in flight with micrometre accuracy.
The drive laser is a multi-hundred-kilowatt CO₂ amplifier chain built by Trumpf, among the most powerful industrial lasers made.
Conversion efficiency from laser energy to usable in-band EUV is only a few percent, which is why the whole machine consumes about a megawatt.
A collector mirror gathers the light; tin debris slowly degrades it, making collector life a key uptime metric.
k: power draw of one EUV scanner
x: One company makes the source, one makes the drive laser, one makes the optics. Each is effectively irreplaceable on any relevant timescale.

DUV excimer lasers, EUV source research

s: The smoothest surfaces humans make
w: EUV is absorbed by everything, including glass and air, so the whole optical path is mirrors in vacuum. Zeiss polishes these mirrors to a figure error that, scaled to the size of Germany, would leave no bump taller than a millimetre.
h: Each mirror is a Mo/Si multilayer on an ultra-low-expansion substrate, reflecting only about 70% of incident EUV.
With six or more mirrors in the path, less than a fifth of the generated light reaches the wafer.
High-NA optics use a 0.55 numerical aperture with anamorphic magnification, halving the printable field and requiring stitching.
Mirror figure, thermal control and vibration isolation together set the achievable overlay, now under a nanometre.
x: Zeiss SMT is a true monopoly on EUV optics, and ASML owns a stake in it. There is no credible second source anywhere.

s: The most complex machine in commerce
w: The scanner is where everything converges: source, optics, mask stage, wafer stage, all moving in synchrony while printing features far smaller than the wavelength used. It is also the single most valuable capital good in the industry.
h: Wafer and reticle stages move in opposite directions at high speed with nanometre-level synchronisation, hundreds of times per wafer.
Immersion DUV puts water between lens and wafer to raise the effective numerical aperture — still the workhorse for most layers.
EUV removes the need for the elaborate multi-patterning schemes DUV requires at tight pitches, cutting steps and cycle time.
High-NA is entering production first at Intel for 14A, with TSMC deferring adoption to a later node.
k: list price of a High-NA EUV system
x: ASML is a hard monopoly in EUV and dominant in immersion DUV. Export controls on these machines are the sharpest instrument in technology policy.
co: EUV, High-NA and immersion DUV scanners

s: Chemistry that remembers where the light was
w: Photoresist records the aerial image as a solubility change. At EUV doses, statistics start to bite: too few photons per feature and line edges get ragged, so resist design is a fight between sensitivity, resolution and roughness.
h: Chemically amplified resists use a photoacid generator so that one absorbed photon triggers many deprotection events.
Metal-oxide resists absorb EUV far more strongly, improving dose efficiency and resolution at the cost of new integration challenges.
The coat-develop track handles the wafer before and after exposure and is tightly clustered with the scanner.
The RLS trade-off — resolution, line-edge roughness, sensitivity — is the central unsolved tension of EUV patterning.
k: tracks are usually paired one-to-one with scanners
x: Japanese chemical firms hold most of the resist market; metal-oxide resist supply from a single Oregon start-up became strategically interesting very quickly.

s: Seeing what is too small to see
w: You cannot fix what you cannot measure. Overlay, critical dimension, film thickness and defectivity are measured on every lot, increasingly with electron beams because optical wavelengths are far larger than the features in question.
h: Scatterometry infers three-dimensional profiles from how light diffracts off periodic structures, without imaging them directly.
E-beam inspection finds killer defects at resolutions optics cannot reach, but is slow, so sampling strategy is a science.
X-ray metrology is being adopted for buried structures such as high-aspect-ratio memory holes and nanosheet stacks.
Data from metrology feeds run-to-run control loops that adjust the next lot's process automatically.

of lots sampled for critical layers
for a full e-beam inspection of one wafer
x: KLA holds a commanding share of process control. Its tools are on every export-control list that matters.

s: Building the chip one atomic layer at a time
w: Every material in a chip is deposited: gate dielectrics, metal gates, barriers, liners, conductors, insulators, hard masks. As geometries shrink, conformality matters more than speed, which is why atomic layer deposition has gone from exotic to routine.
h: Chemical vapour deposition grows films from reacting gases; plasma-enhanced variants lower the temperature enough to protect what is already there.
Atomic layer deposition alternates self-limiting precursor and reactant pulses, giving perfect step coverage in deep, narrow features.
Physical vapour deposition sputters metal from a target and remains the workhorse for thicker conductive films.
Selective deposition — growing film only on chosen surfaces — is the emerging trick for reducing patterning steps.
k: deposition steps in a leading-edge flow
aspect ratios ALD must coat conformally
x: A short list of tool vendors, and each recipe is qualified to a specific chamber. Swapping suppliers mid-node is not realistic.

s: Removing material with atomic discipline
w: Etch translates the resist pattern into the underlying film. Modern etch is plasma chemistry tuned so precisely that it can remove one material and stop dead on another, or peel off a single atomic layer per cycle.
h: Reactive ion etching accelerates ions to the surface for directionality while radicals provide chemical selectivity.
Atomic layer etching splits the process into self-limiting modification and removal steps, mirroring ALD in reverse.
3D NAND requires etching holes with aspect ratios beyond 60:1 straight through hundreds of layers without bowing or twisting.
Selectivity, profile control and chamber matching across a fleet are the practical differentiators.
k: aspect ratio for 3D NAND channel holes
share of process steps that are etch
x: Lam and TEL dominate the hardest etch applications. High-aspect-ratio etch capability is a direct gate on memory scaling.

s: Flatten, rinse, repeat
w: Every few layers the wafer must be made perfectly flat again or the next lithography step will not focus. Chemical-mechanical polishing does this with a rotating pad, an engineered slurry, and enormous process control.
h: CMP combines chemical softening with mechanical abrasion; the slurry chemistry differs per material — copper, tungsten, oxide, nitride.
Dishing and erosion are the characteristic defects, controlled by pattern density rules imposed back on the designer.
Post-CMP cleaning removes slurry residue and particles, itself a specialised wet process.
Single-wafer cleaning tools handle hundreds of steps per flow, from resist strip to final rinse.
k: CMP steps in a leading-edge flow
total process steps for advanced logic
x: Competitive on tools, sticky on consumables. The slurry, pad and clean chemistry are qualified together as one system.

s: Firing dopants in, then healing the damage
w: Doping sets where a semiconductor conducts. Ions are accelerated into the lattice at precise energy and dose, which wrecks the crystal locally, so the wafer is then annealed just long enough to restore order without letting the dopants wander.
h: Implant energy sets depth and dose sets concentration; angle matters enormously in three-dimensional transistor structures.
Millisecond and laser-spike anneals heat the surface for a flash so dopant diffusion is minimised.
Ultra-shallow junctions in nanosheet devices push both implant and anneal toward their physical limits.
Selective epitaxial growth of doped source/drain has replaced implant for some of the most critical junctions.
x: Mature, concentrated, and rarely a headline — but implant angle control is one of the harder problems in gate-all-around integration.

s: Ten thousand wafers moving in the dark
w: A modern fab is a logistics problem wearing a cleanroom suit. Overhead vehicles shuttle sealed wafer carriers between hundreds of tools; scheduling, dispatch and fault detection software decide which lot goes where, continuously.
h: Automated material handling systems move FOUPs on ceiling tracks with no human contact for the entire three-month cycle.
Fault detection and classification watches thousands of sensor traces per tool to catch drift before it scraps product.
Run-to-run control adjusts recipes lot by lot using metrology feedback.
Machine learning is now used for scheduling, chamber matching and virtual metrology, cutting cycle time measurably.
k: cycle time for a leading-edge wafer
wafer starts per month at a large fab
x: Software and know-how rather than hardware, but yield learning rate is the single biggest driver of foundry profitability.

s: From fins to stacked nanosheets
w: The FinFET, which carried the industry for a decade, has given way to gate-all-around nanosheets: horizontal ribbons of silicon completely wrapped by gate material, giving better electrostatic control and a tunable width that FinFETs could only quantise.
h: Nanosheet width can be varied continuously, letting designers trade drive current against area cell by cell — TSMC calls this NanoFlex.
Inner spacers must be formed in cavities etched between stacked sheets, one of the hardest integration steps in the flow.
Work-function metal stacks set threshold voltage and must be deposited into gaps only a few nanometres wide.
Complementary FET, stacking n and p devices vertically, is the research direction beyond nanosheets.
k: typical performance gain per node step
first TSMC nanosheet node, volume from late 2025
x: Only three companies are attempting leading-edge logic. Each new node costs more and delivers less scaling than the last.

s: Rewiring the chip from underneath
w: Traditionally signal and power wires share the same crowded stack above the transistors. Backside power delivery moves the power network to the underside of a thinned wafer, cutting voltage droop and freeing the front side for signals.
h: The wafer is bonded to a carrier, thinned to a few hundred nanometres, and a power network is built on the exposed back.
Nano-through-silicon vias connect front-side devices to backside rails.
Intel's PowerVia shipped first at 18A; TSMC's Super Power Rail arrives with A16.
Gains are largest for power-hungry designs — precisely the AI accelerator profile.
k: typical performance uplift from backside power
x: A genuine differentiator that reshuffles the competitive order, and a thermally awkward one: heat now has to leave through the signal side.

s: The copper is now the problem
w: Above the transistors sit fifteen or more metal layers. As wires get thinner, electron scattering makes copper resistivity rise sharply, and the barrier layer that keeps copper out of the silicon eats an ever larger fraction of the wire's cross-section.
h: Damascene processing etches trenches, fills them with copper by electroplating, then polishes back — copper cannot be etched cleanly.
At the tightest pitches the industry is switching to ruthenium or molybdenum, which need little or no barrier and win despite higher bulk resistivity.
Low-k and air-gap dielectrics reduce capacitance but are mechanically fragile during packaging.
Interconnect RC delay, not transistor speed, now limits performance in many designs.
k: metal layers on an advanced logic die
resistivity rise for copper at the tightest pitches
materials replacing copper at the lowest levels
x: A materials problem with no clean answer. Every candidate replacement brings new integration and reliability questions.

s: Where the economics actually live
w: Defect density decides whether a node makes money. On a reticle-sized die, a small change in defects per square centimetre swings yield dramatically, which is why big accelerators are split into chiplets and why every part is sold in performance bins.
h: Yield learning follows a predictable curve; the rate of learning, not the starting point, determines who wins a node.
Large dies are punished superlinearly by defects, which is the core economic argument for chiplets.
Redundancy — spare cores, spare SRAM rows, spare HBM channels — recovers parts that would otherwise be scrap.
Binning turns a yield distribution into a product ladder, with the best silicon sold at the top of the stack.

x: Yield is the most closely guarded number in the industry, and the one that decides whether an accelerator programme is viable.

s: Three companies at the leading edge, one that matters most
w: Fabless design and merchant manufacturing separated in the 1990s and the leading edge has consolidated ever since. Today one company makes almost every advanced AI accelerator on Earth, on an island whose political status is the industry's largest tail risk.
h: TSMC runs N2 in volume with A16 following in the second half of 2026 and capacity growing at roughly 70% a year through 2028.
Samsung and Intel Foundry compete for the remainder, with Intel betting on 18A and High-NA-enabled 14A.
Mature nodes — 28 nm and above — remain enormous, and Chinese capacity expansion there is reshaping pricing.
Geographic diversification into Arizona, Japan and Germany is real but adds cost and lags Taiwan on both yield and scale.

x: The single greatest concentration risk in the world economy. Almost every frontier accelerator is made within a few dozen kilometres of the same coastline.

s: A capacitor, a transistor, and a refresh timer
w: Every DRAM bit is a charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks and must be topped up thousands of times a second. Shrinking that capacitor while keeping enough charge to read reliably has been the industry's core difficulty for thirty years.

s: The scarcest thing in AI hardware
w: HBM stacks DRAM dies vertically over through-silicon vias and mounts them beside the processor on an interposer, trading a narrow fast bus for an extraordinarily wide one. It is the component that decides how large a model a chip can hold and how fast it can stream weights.
h: HBM4 doubles the interface to 2,048 bits and 32 channels, with per-pin rates above 11 Gb/s and stack bandwidth beyond 2.8 TB/s.
The logic base die at the bottom of the stack is now made on a foundry logic process, which turns memory makers into foundry customers.
Twelve-high stacks are standard and sixteen-high is being qualified; wafer thinning and warpage control are the limiting arts.
Hybrid bonding is expected to replace microbumps as stack heights grow and thermal budgets tighten.

s: Hundreds of layers, cents per gigabyte

String stacking builds the array in two or more decks because the etch cannot go deeper in one pass.
CMOS-under-array and bonded-array designs move periphery logic out of the way to raise density.
Controller firmware — wear levelling, error correction, garbage collection — determines real-world endurance far more than the raw cells.

s: The real bottleneck on AI supply
w: An accelerator is not one chip. Logic dies and HBM stacks are placed side by side on a silicon interposer that carries tens of thousands of fine connections between them, then mounted on an organic substrate. This is CoWoS, and its capacity — not lithography — has been the binding constraint on AI hardware.
h: CoWoS-S uses a silicon interposer; CoWoS-L uses local silicon bridges in an organic matrix to reach much larger package sizes.
Package area is measured in reticle multiples: 5.5× is in volume production, with 14× and twenty HBM stacks on the roadmap.
Warpage, thermal mismatch and underfill behaviour get harder with every increase in package area.
Alternatives — Intel EMIB, Samsung I-Cube, Amkor and ASE offerings — provide overflow but not at equivalent scale.

s: Copper welded to copper, no bumps
w: Instead of connecting dies with solder microbumps, hybrid bonding fuses copper pads and surrounding dielectric directly, at pitches ten times finer. It is how cache is stacked on processors and how future HBM stacks will be built.
h: Surfaces are polished to sub-nanometre flatness, aligned, bonded at room temperature, then annealed so the copper expands and welds.
Pitch drives density: TSMC's SoIC is in production around 9 µm with 6 µm planned and 4.5 µm on the roadmap.
Stacking removes the bump resistance and inductance, cutting interconnect energy dramatically.
Thermal design is the hard part — heat from a lower die must now escape through an upper one.

s: Finding the bad ones before they cost more

s: Thousands of small matrix engines, fed

The memory hierarchy — registers, shared memory, L2, HBM — is designed so that operands arrive without stalling the arithmetic.

s: Buying accuracy back with fewer bits
w: Precision is the cheapest lever in the stack. Every halving of bit width roughly doubles arithmetic throughput and halves memory traffic, so the industry has walked from FP32 down through FP16 and FP8 to four-bit block formats, inventing scaling tricks to keep training stable.

Microscaling formats such as MXFP8 and MXFP4 have been standardised through the Open Compute Project.
Training typically keeps master weights and some reductions in higher precision while doing the bulk of matrix work low.
Inference tolerates lower precision than training, which is why serving stacks quantise aggressively.

s: Buying back the margin
w: If you buy a million accelerators a year, designing your own becomes rational. Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium, Meta's MTIA and Microsoft's Maia are all systolic-array designs built at TSMC with a partner doing the physical implementation.

Hyperscalers rarely build these alone — Broadcom and Marvell supply the SerDes, packaging and physical design expertise.
The economics work when a single workload is large and stable enough to amortise a multi-hundred-million-dollar programme.
Frontier labs have begun commissioning their own parts too, extending the pattern beyond the classic hyperscalers.

The commercial difficulty is rarely the silicon — it is the software ecosystem and the pace at which model architectures move.

Memory bandwidth, not compute, limits on-device model size — which is why quantisation and small-model research matter commercially.
Hybrid designs run a small model locally and escalate to the cloud only when needed.

s: Ethernet finally beat InfiniBand at its own game

s: Where the physical economy meets the model
w: Logistics routing, demand forecasting, quality inspection, energy dispatch, mining, agriculture and construction all use AI in ways that predate the language-model wave and are being reshaped by it. Value here is measured in operating margin, not tokens.
h: Vision inspection on production lines was one of the earliest profitable deployments of deep learning.
Forecasting and optimisation benefit from foundation models mostly through easier interfaces and better handling of unstructured inputs.
Domain data — sensor histories, maintenance logs, process recipes — is the scarce asset, and it is owned by incumbents.
Industrial deployments require determinism and auditability that general assistants do not provide.
k: annual savings reported from single large routing deployments
the scarce asset in industrial AI
the requirement that rules out naive LLM use
x: Fragmented and unglamorous, but this is where AI touches the majority of the physical economy.

s: The most consequential customer
w: Governments are large buyers of AI for intelligence analysis, logistics, cyber defence and autonomy. Frontier labs have moved from refusing this market to serving it under specific usage policies, which is itself one of the notable shifts of the past two years.
h: Classified deployments require air-gapped or accredited environments and dedicated model variants.
Intelligence analysis — summarising, translating and cross-referencing at volume — is the least contested use case.
Autonomy in weapons remains policy-constrained and is the sharpest ethical boundary in the sector.
Procurement timelines and accreditation regimes were not built for a technology that ships every few months.
k: the deployment requirement for classified work
how labs constrain permitted government use
between procurement cycles and model release cadence
x: Politically sensitive, commercially significant, and the area where usage policies are tested hardest.

s: Vision, language, action
w: Instead of programming a robot per task, a single model maps camera images and an instruction to motor commands. The bet is that robotics can have its own scaling moment once enough manipulation data exists to train on.
h: Vision-language-action models reuse pretrained visual and language representations and add an action head.
Teleoperation demonstrations remain the primary data source, and collecting them is slow and expensive.
Simulation with domain randomisation generates volume, but the reality gap in contact-rich manipulation is stubborn.
Generalisation across robot embodiments is the key open question — one brain, many bodies.
k: of teleoperation per useful manipulation skill
the persistent gap in contact-rich tasks
the goal that would change the economics
x: Data-limited rather than compute-limited, which is the reverse of language models and makes progress harder to buy.

s: Motors, gearboxes and the hard physics
w: The intelligence is improving faster than the hardware. Humanoids and manipulators are limited by actuator torque density, battery energy, tactile sensing and the cost of building a reliable machine that survives thousands of hours of contact.
h: Actuator choice — harmonic drives, cycloidal gearboxes, quasi-direct-drive — sets the compliance and force control a robot can achieve.
Tactile and force sensing is where robotics is furthest from human capability and where manipulation most often fails.
Battery energy density caps untethered operating time, which shapes what tasks are economically viable.
Rare-earth magnets in the motors tie robotics directly back to the critical-minerals chokepoint.
k: magnets linking robotics to rare earth supply
x: Chinese suppliers dominate the actuator, reducer and magnet supply chain, which makes Western humanoid programmes structurally dependent.

s: The longest-running deployment of embodied AI
w: Self-driving is the most mature physical AI application, with driverless commercial services operating in multiple cities. It took far longer than anyone predicted, which is the most useful data point the field has produced about deploying autonomy safely.
h: Sensor philosophies diverge sharply — lidar-and-radar redundancy versus camera-only — with real cost and capability consequences.
End-to-end learned driving policies have displaced much of the hand-written planning stack.
Safety cases require enormous validated mileage and rigorous scenario coverage before regulators permit removal of the driver.
Unit economics depend on remote assistance ratios, depot costs and utilisation, not just on the technology working.
k: from first serious programmes to commercial service
the ratio that decides operating cost
x: A useful reality check for every claim about agentic autonomy: capability demos are years away from safe deployment.

s: How machines see and feel
w: Cameras, lidar, radar, tactile arrays and inertial units are the input side of physical AI. Sensor cost curves have fallen steeply, which is a large part of why autonomy became commercially plausible at all.
h: Automotive lidar has fallen from tens of thousands of dollars to hundreds through solid-state designs and volume.
Image sensors with high dynamic range are essential for driving into low sun and out of tunnels.
Tactile sensing — vision-based skins, capacitive arrays — remains immature relative to the manipulation problem it must solve.
Sensor fusion and time synchronisation across modalities is an underrated engineering problem.
k: fall in automotive lidar unit cost
x: Chinese suppliers dominate volume lidar and many sensor categories, with the same geopolitical exposure as the rest of the hardware chain.

s: Practising where mistakes are free
w: Robots and vehicles learn most of what they know in simulation, because real-world data collection is slow, dangerous and expensive. Fidelity, and specifically contact physics, determines how much of that learning transfers.
h: Physics engines must model friction, deformation and collision accurately enough that learned policies survive the reality gap.
Domain randomisation varies textures, lighting and dynamics so policies do not overfit to simulated appearance.
Neural reconstruction builds simulation environments directly from real captured scenes.
Scenario generation for safety validation deliberately searches for rare, dangerous situations.
k: what safety validation must generate deliberately
x: Increasingly bundled with accelerator platforms, which quietly extends GPU vendor influence into robotics.

s: Chat was a starting point, not an answer
w: The interface determines what people can actually do with a model. Chat is general but weak at structure; canvases, IDEs, spreadsheets and agent inboxes each fit different work, and the design vocabulary for AI products is still being invented.
h: Streaming, interruption and visible reasoning changed expectations about what a computer interaction feels like.
Artifacts and canvases separate the conversation from the thing being produced, which fits iterative work far better.
Delegation interfaces — queue a task, come back later — suit long-running agents better than synchronous chat.
Trust affordances such as citations, diffs and undo matter more than raw capability for adoption.
k: the interaction change users noticed first
x: Not a chokepoint, but the layer where most of the value is either delivered or squandered.

s: Phones, laptops, glasses and the last centimetre
w: Hardware is where AI reaches people. Phones and laptops now ship neural processors and local models; glasses and wearables promise ambient assistance and raise the sharpest privacy questions of any form factor.
h: On-device inference gives latency and privacy benefits and is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute.
Hybrid architectures run small models locally and escalate to the cloud, which requires careful handling of what leaves the device.
Smart glasses combine cameras, microphones and displays in a socially visible package, which is a norms problem as much as a technical one.
Operating system integration determines which assistant a user actually reaches for.
k: the real limit on local model size
x: Distribution power sits with a very small number of platform owners, which shapes the entire application layer above it.

s: Who decides what a billion people touch
w: App stores, browsers, operating systems and cloud marketplaces sit between models and users. Default placement and bundling have historically decided technology markets more reliably than product quality, and there is no reason to expect this one to differ.
h: Cloud marketplaces let enterprises buy models against existing committed spend, which is a large and underappreciated advantage.
Bundling AI into existing productivity subscriptions changes the comparison from 'is this worth paying for' to 'is this worth switching from'.
Browser and OS-level assistants intercept intent before the user reaches any application.
Regulatory attention to self-preferencing and bundling is following the same path it took in previous platform cycles.
k: the fastest route to scale for incumbents
x: The most reliable predictor of which model people use is not benchmarks — it is what is already installed.

s: The largest private build-out in history
w: Roughly $690–725bn of hyperscaler capital expenditure was guided for 2026, up sharply again, and that figure excludes the private labs and neoclouds. It is being financed with cash flow, corporate debt, asset-backed securities, private credit and vendor arrangements.
h: Depreciation schedules are the swing variable: extending assumed useful life flatters earnings and is contested by short sellers.
Circular arrangements — vendors investing in customers who buy their product — recur and complicate reading demand signals.
Asset-backed structures secured on GPUs and leases move risk to credit markets that price it differently from equity.
Concentration in public indices means a repricing of a few names would be felt far beyond technology.
k: of that directed at AI infrastructure
x: The financing structure, not the technology, is the most plausible source of a sharp discontinuity in the build-out.

s: The periodic table as policy instrument
w: Advanced computing is now governed by an interlocking set of controls: on lithography tools, on accelerators, on high-bandwidth memory, on EDA software, and — from the other direction — on critical minerals. The rules change often and retroactively reshape company strategy.
h: Controls target chokepoints rather than end products, which is why lithography and EDA are the primary levers.
China's mineral export licensing is the mirror-image instrument, aimed at inputs the West cannot quickly replace.
Country-tier frameworks determine which nations can host large clusters and under what security conditions.
Enforcement is imperfect — transshipment, die banks and third-country routing have all been documented.
k: what controls target rather than products
the structure controls have now taken
x: The single largest source of discontinuity risk in the industry. A rule change can strand billions of dollars overnight.
co: US Bureau of Industry and Security

s: Three continents, three philosophies
w: The EU regulates by risk category and obligation, the United States by sector, agency and state law, and China by licensing and content control. Companies deploying globally must satisfy all three at once, which mostly means satisfying the strictest.
h: The EU AI Act imposes tiered obligations with specific rules for general-purpose models above a compute threshold.
US regulation is fragmented across agencies and states, with several state laws imposing real compliance burdens.
China requires algorithm registration and security review before public-facing generative services launch.
Standards bodies are quietly doing much of the substantive work on evaluation, provenance and risk management.
x: Compliance cost falls hardest on smaller developers, which tends to entrench the largest players regardless of intent.

s: Unresolved questions worth billions
w: Whether training on copyrighted material is permitted, whether model outputs can be copyrighted, and who is liable when an output infringes are all still being decided in courts across several jurisdictions — with divergent early answers.
h: Fair use and text-and-data-mining exceptions are the central legal arguments, and they differ substantially by jurisdiction.
Output similarity, memorisation and regurgitation are treated separately from the legality of training itself.
Indemnification has become a standard commercial term, with providers absorbing customer risk to enable adoption.
Licensing markets have grown partly as a hedge against unfavourable rulings, not only as a source of better data.
x: A genuinely binary risk. Different rulings would produce very different industry structures.

s: A few thousand people, priced accordingly
w: The number of people who have trained a frontier model end to end is small enough to fit in a large lecture hall. Compensation packages for that group have reached levels normally associated with professional sport, and acquisition-by-hiring has become a standard structure.
h: Scarce specialisms cluster in pretraining infrastructure, RL, kernel engineering and large-scale systems reliability.
Acquihire-style deals let acquirers take a team and licence technology without a conventional acquisition review.
Talent concentration compounds: the best people go where the compute is, which is where the best people already are.
Adjacent shortages — electricians, pipefitters, substation engineers — are more binding in practice and far less discussed.
k: people who have run frontier-scale pretraining
the shortage that actually delays build-outs
x: Compute can be bought and power can be built. The people who know how to use both cannot be conjured on the same timescale.

s: The point of the whole chain
w: At the top of the stack a person or organisation either gets something worth more than they paid or does not. So far the clearest measurable returns accrue to individual users and to a handful of infrastructure suppliers; enterprise-level returns are real but unevenly realised.
h: Individual productivity gains are well documented in coding, writing, support and analysis, and vary enormously by task.
Enterprise returns depend on process redesign, not tool deployment, which is why many pilots do not convert.
The clearest profits so far sit with the hardware and infrastructure layers rather than with model providers or applications.
Consumer surplus — value received but not paid for — is large and mostly invisible in economic statistics.
k: time saving reported by users of one legal AI product
how consumer surplus appears in GDP
x: The open question of the entire cycle: whether the value created at this layer justifies the capital deployed twenty-six layers below.
co: Free and subscription users at scale

s: What the chain does to the people in it
w: The effects are unevenly distributed and hard to measure. Entry-level work in some categories is contracting, annotation work has created a large and contested labour market, and the information environment is absorbing generated content at a scale nobody planned for.
h: Task-level automation is uneven — some jobs are augmented, some restructured, few eliminated wholesale in the short run.
Entry-level roles are most exposed because they concentrate the routine tasks that models handle best.
Annotation and moderation labour is globally distributed and has documented psychological and wage concerns.
Synthetic content at scale changes what evidence means, which is a slow-acting externality with no obvious owner.
x: The externality most likely to determine the political durability of the whole build-out.

s: The bill the atmosphere gets
w: Data centre electricity demand is projected to more than double by 2030. Whether that is a climate problem depends almost entirely on what generates the electricity, and on whether efficiency gains outrun demand growth — historically they have not.
h: Jevons dynamics apply: cheaper inference has expanded usage far faster than efficiency has reduced per-token energy.
Location and generation mix matter more than facility efficiency for actual emissions.
Twenty-four-seven carbon-free matching is a much stricter standard than annual renewable matching, and few operators meet it.
Embodied carbon in construction, silicon and equipment is significant and inconsistently reported.
k: projected global data centre demand by 2030
the emissions category most often omitted
x: Efficiency improvements are real and consistently outpaced by demand growth. Absolute consumption is what matters.

s: Where the silicon goes to die
w: Accelerators do not last forever, and the industry has not settled on how long they last. Retired hardware moves to secondary markets, gets refurbished, or enters a global e-waste stream from which copper, gold and rare earths are imperfectly recovered.
h: Older accelerators retain real value for inference and fine-tuning long after they leave frontier training duty.
A liquid secondary market exists but is opaque, and residual values are the key uncertainty in neocloud financing.
Formal recycling recovers copper, gold, palladium and some rare earths; informal processing recovers less and harms more.
Facilities designed for one rack generation may be stranded by the next, which is a larger write-off risk than the chips themselves.
k: annual global e-waste, of which a minority is formally recycled
contested economic life of an AI accelerator
the risk to facilities, not just to hardware
x: Closing the loop on materials would relieve pressure at the very bottom of this chain. Recovery rates today are far too low for that.
